If the knights of ren decided to turn against the first order as a third party, would it be in character, and a clever move, for Hux to disguise a thermal detonator as a holocron, and putting it on

message.content: It can be in character, but only if Hux is written as a pragmatic enemy of the Order rather than a Sith-like ritualist. The Knights of Ren already operate outside normal First Order military discipline, so their turn against the Order as a third party is plausible. Hux would be the most credible person to cross that line if he believes the Order’s bureaucracy is holding the future of the Empire hostage. A detonator disguised as a holocron fits him better than a lightsaber duel or mystical prophecy because it turns his access to ceremonial objects and his contempt for “soft” Sith mysticism into a weapon. It is a clever move if it is framed as a one-time tactical trap rather than a recurring scheme. A thermal detonator hidden in a holocron shell would exploit the audience’s expectation that holocrons are sacred, fragile, or valuable, making the detonation both surprising and thematically bitter. Assuming “putting it on” means presenting or placing it, the trick becomes smarter if the Ren accept it because they expect Hux to offer a symbol of legitimacy, or if Hux uses it to frame another faction inside the First Order. That makes it feel like a calculated deception instead of a random explosion. It is less in character if Hux does it for sheer theatrical malice, because Hux’s strength is ideology, not subtlety. Hux would be more likely to make a public declaration, sabotage a fleet, or use a ceremony as a political coup than to quietly poison a holocron unless that act directly serves a larger argument against the Supreme Leader or the Order’s old ways. The deception should feel like a compromise between his bluntness and the Ren’s mysticism: he understands them poorly, but he understands enough to use their reverence for objects, lineage, and “chosen” symbols against them. If the scene makes it look like Hux has become a cunning dark-side manipulator beyond his established psychology, it will feel out of character. In short, yes: it works best when it is a desperate, calculated betrayal by a military ideologue using a religious object as a Trojan horse. The clearest way to write it is to give Hux a clear motive, make the disguised detonator a symbol rather than just a bomb, and let the consequence be political rather than merely explosive. For example, Hux could place it in the holocron he presents to the Knights of Ren during a ceremony, hoping the Ren will treat it as a relic while the detonator turns it into a public act of rebellion. That would make the move clever, in character, and thematically connected to the Knights’ break with the First Order.
